## Chapter 67: Advanced Control Charts

### Common Control Chart Types and When to Use Them

**X-bar & R Chart**

- The data is variable (continuous)
- The data can be grouped into subgroups, letting you plot each group's average
- Average output per hour
- Average phone response speed per hour
- Average number of customers per day
- Defects per hour
- The data count in each subgroup is under 8 (though you can use the X-bar & R chart for subgroup sizes up to 100 in Minitab)
- Presents two charts
- The X-bar control chart plots each subgroup's mean
- The R chart plots the range

<img alt="Example Xbar-R chart, with the X-bar chart above and the R chart below" src="data:image/png;base64," style="max-width:700px;width:100%;height:auto;display:block;margin:0.6rem auto;"  />


<img alt="Example Xbar-S chart, with the X-bar chart above and the S chart below" src="data:image/png;base64," style="max-width:700px;width:100%;height:auto;display:block;margin:0.6rem auto;"  />


**X-bar & S Chart**

- The data is variable (continuous)
- The data can be grouped into subgroups, letting you plot each group's average
- The data count in each subgroup is over 8
- Sigma can be easily calculated (otherwise, use X-bar & R)
- Presents two charts
- The X-bar control chart plots each subgroup's mean
- The S chart plots the standard deviation

**I & MR Chart**

- The data is variable (continuous)
- The data can't easily be grouped into reasonable subgroups, so you need to track individual data points instead of subgroup averages
- The data is very hard or expensive to obtain
- Production is very slow, so waiting for enough data to build subgroups would take too long (for example, tracking data on surgeries performed at a small outpatient clinic)
- The products have a low cycle time

<img alt="Example I-MR chart, with the individual-value chart above and the moving-range chart below" src="data:image/png;base64," style="max-width:700px;width:100%;height:auto;display:block;margin:0.6rem auto;"  />


**P Chart**

- The data is discrete
- The data is presented as a percentage (percent defective), rather than a count
- Doesn't require a constant sample/subgroup size
- Plots the proportion of nonconforming units (those that are defective, don't meet specifications)
- Use when:
- it's impossible, too time-consuming, or financially impractical to measure or analyze numeric measurements
- the sample or subgroup sizes aren't equal, so the percentage defective matters more than the number of defects per group (since you can't accurately compare numbers from a smaller group with numbers from a larger group)
- the data is rate-based, because it comes from a binomial or attribute process: the measurement or process is pass/fail, go/no-go, etc. You can't plot a 1 or 0 on a control chart, but you can plot the percentage of 1s or 0s in each sample.

<img alt="Example P chart" src="data:image/png;base64," style="max-width:700px;width:100%;height:auto;display:block;margin:0.6rem auto;"  />


<img alt="Example NP chart" src="data:image/png;base64," style="max-width:700px;width:100%;height:auto;display:block;margin:0.6rem auto;"  />


**NP Chart**

- The data is discrete
- The data is presented as a percentage (percent defective), rather than a count
- Requires a constant sample size to be useful; otherwise, you can use it for anything you'd use a P chart for
- Plots the number of nonconforming units in each sample size

**U Chart**

- The data is discrete
- The data is presented as a count (number of defects)
- Doesn't require a constant sample/subgroup size
- Plots the number of defects per unit
- Use when the data is about the defects themselves, not the overall defective product

<img alt="Example U chart" src="data:image/png;base64," style="max-width:700px;width:100%;height:auto;display:block;margin:0.6rem auto;"  />


<img alt="Example C chart" src="data:image/png;base64," style="max-width:700px;width:100%;height:auto;display:block;margin:0.6rem auto;"  />


**C Chart**

- The data is discrete
- The data is presented as a count (number of defects)
- Requires a constant sample/subgroup size
- Plots the number of defects per sample
- Use when the data is about the defects themselves, not the overall defective product

### Creating and Reading Control Charts in Minitab

**X-bar & R or X-bar & S Charts**

To better understand the X-bar & R chart process in Minitab, consider a real-world scenario. A call center is tracking the number of calls on hold. The call center randomly logs the number of calls on hold at a given moment, five times an hour. This data is presented below, for a 10-hour shift (Hour and Calls on Hold columns, with 5 measurements per hour across 10 hours).

Copy this information into Minitab, if you're following along with the analysis on your own. If you're not sure how to use Minitab's basic data entry or navigation functions, see Chapter 102 for additional information.

Every control chart is found under **Stat → Control Charts**. For Xbar-R: Stat → Control Charts → Variables Charts for Subgroups → Xbar-R.

This option instructs Minitab to run the control tests covered in Chapter 38. If a data point or series of data points on the control chart fails any of these tests, Minitab will highlight them in red, making it easier for Six Sigma specialists to spot whether a process might be out of control.

This option instructs Minitab to run the control tests covered in Chapter 38. If a data point or series of data points on the control chart fails any of these tests, Minitab will highlight them in red, making it easier for Six Sigma specialists to spot whether a process might be out of control.

Click OK on the options dialog box. Click OK on the Xbar-R chart dialog box. Minitab generates a chart and a text description of any control tests that failed.

```
Test Results for R Chart of Calls On Hold

<img alt="Xbar-R chart of Calls on Hold, with point 2 on the R chart flagged for failing the test" src="data:image/png;base64," style="max-width:700px;width:100%;height:auto;display:block;margin:0.6rem auto;"  />


TEST 1. One point more than 3.00 standard deviations from center line.
Test Failed at points:  2

```

You can see above that the range control chart failed at point 2 — one point is beyond 3 standard deviations from the center line. Every other point is within control parameters, and the sample average (x-bar) chart is also under control. This means the average number of calls on hold within each hour was under control. However, apart from hour 2, the specific data points varied much more than in other hours, meaning one or more collected samples was very high.

Someone looking at this chart would probably not consider the process fully out of control, but would want to investigate hour 2's samples. What happened to cause a drastic shift in the range? Was a number logged incorrectly? Did several employees take short, unplanned breaks that caused a sudden spike in calls on hold? Control charts can point to small problems like these before they turn into bigger, systemic problems.

The steps for building an X-bar & S chart are the same as described above, except you'd start with Stat > Control Charts > Variables Charts for Subgroups > Xbar-S.

**I-MR Chart**

The I-MR chart (individual and moving range) is used when you aren't grouping data into subgroups. Either it isn't feasible to collect enough samples for subgrouping, or it's important, for some reason, to view the chart at the individual data-point level.

For example, a mid-sized car dealership wants to measure the number of sales closed daily. Most dealerships don't close hundreds of sales a day, so tracking by hour or in batch sizes won't provide much information for a single month's data. If you're looking at a full year's data, the dealership could group by week; otherwise, the I-MR chart is a good option.

To follow along with this example, copy the sales data below into Minitab (22 daily values, ranging from 15 to 24 closed sales).

Select Stat → Control Charts → Variables Charts for Individuals → I-MR (same menu as the diagram above).

Complete similar steps to those done for the X-bar & R chart:

1. Click the box under "Variables."
2. Click "Sales closed daily" in the column list and click Select.
3. Click I-MR Options.
4. Click Tests.
5. In the dropdown, select "Perform all tests for special causes."
6. Click OK.
7. Click OK.

Minitab generates the I-MR chart and data on whether any test failed.

```
Test Results for MR Chart of Sales closed daily

<img alt="I-MR chart of daily closed sales, with point 16 on the moving-range chart flagged" src="data:image/png;base64," style="max-width:700px;width:100%;height:auto;display:block;margin:0.6rem auto;"  />


TEST 1. One point more than 3.00 standard deviations from center line.
Test Failed at points:  16

```

In this specific case, the number of sales per month, shown on the upper individuals chart, is under control. The moving range — how much change there is between each day's numbers — is under control, except at point 16. If you look at the data, you'll see that, between point 16 and point 17, there's a difference of 8 sales. This is the point with the biggest difference between consecutive daily data points, which likely explains the test failure.

A dealership or Six Sigma team working with this data probably wouldn't be too worried about this single point. Thinking about it practically, it might be that some sales that maybe started the day before didn't close, which artificially inflated the day's numbers and caused the sudden, wider-than-normal spread. In this case, the dealership or Six Sigma team would simply note the point and keep an eye on the control chart, for similar test failures down the road that might indicate some kind of pattern or process problem.

**P Chart**

Remember: a P chart is used to track rate-based attribute data. It's probably one of the most widely used attribute-based control charts, because rates are generally easier to work with than raw attribute data, particularly because you don't need to worry about ensuring the same sample or subgroup size. You can also combine several defect types in the same report, because P charts are typically concerned with whether the product, part, or test passed or failed — not the specific details of the defects that caused the pass or fail.

The type of data reported at the management level also tends to be well complemented by the P chart's characteristics. Executive leadership often wants to know audit results, first-run yields, scrap rates, or defect rates, all of which can be illustrated with P charts.

Proportion data is often one of the first types available to Six Sigma teams — even before a Six Sigma team is attached to a process, many operators and business managers capture pass/fail-type data. That means a Six Sigma team can often build a first baseline control chart from proportion data, and watch the rates improve as process improvements are made.

To understand how to build a P chart in Minitab, consider the following real-world scenario. A professional printing company discovers a possible problem with a printing process used to print business cards. Customers are reporting high defect rates. The company starts monitoring the process more closely, reviewing 100 samples daily, to determine whether there's any defect on each printed card. The results are logged in the data table (20 days, each with 100 samples and a defect count ranging from 0 to 9).

Copy this data into Minitab, if you're following along building control charts.

To build a P chart from this data, start by going to Stat → Control Charts → Attribute Charts → P (same Control Charts menu, Attributes branch).

Follow the steps below to enter the data into the dialog box:

1. Click the box under Variables.
2. Click "Defects" in the left column.
3. Click Select, under the left column, to select "Defects" into the Variables box.
4. Click the box next to "Subgroup sizes."
5. Click "Samples" in the left column.
6. Click Select, under the left column, to select "Samples" into the Subgroup box.
7. Click P-Chart Options.

In this case, there's likely a control problem within the process, given the failure at three points. The process owner or Six Sigma team tied to this process will want to investigate both the samples and the process, to find out whether there's an ongoing process problem or a sample-specific issue.

*Notice there are fewer special-cause tests listed than there were for the earlier control charts built. This happens because there are fewer control tests for attribute data. It's been said several times throughout this book that continuous, or variable, data is generally better for statistical analysis than attribute data, and this is one example of why.*

The steps for building other attribute control charts, including NP, U, and C charts, are the same as those used to build the P chart.

#### Worked example across five approaches: X-bar & R Chart (subgroups)

The exact values from the call center table in the text above (5 measurements/hour × 10 hours) aren't available as text — they were only in the figure. For the exercise, we use an **illustrative** data set with the same shape (10 subgroups of 5 calls-on-hold measurements), with a deliberate spike at subgroup 2 to reproduce the same qualitative pattern from the text (range out of control at a single subgroup, means in control):

`H1: 3,4,3,5,4` · `H2: 2,9,3,4,3` · `H3: 4,5,4,3,5` · `H4: 3,4,5,4,3` · `H5: 5,4,3,4,5` · `H6: 4,3,4,5,4` · `H7: 3,5,4,3,4` · `H8: 4,4,3,5,4` · `H9: 5,3,4,4,3` · `H10: 4,4,5,3,4`

<img alt="Excel + Power BI (DAX) illustration of the example: X-bar & R Chart (subgroups)" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64," style="max-width:100%;" />

**Excel 365**: build averages and ranges per subgroup with `=AVERAGE()` and `=MAX()-MIN()` per row, then the average of the averages (X-bar-bar) and the average of the ranges (R-bar). The limits use the standard control constants for n=5: **A2=0.577, D3=0, D4=2.114** (tabulated, not calculated by Excel): `UCLx = X̄̄ + A2·R̄`, `LCLx = X̄̄ − A2·R̄`, `UCLr = D4·R̄`, `LCLr = D3·R̄`.

**Power BI (DAX)** — same tabulated constants (A2/D3/D4 have no DAX formula of their own — they're AIAG/ASTM table values, identical in any tool), applied in native measures:

```dax
X Barra Barra = AVERAGE ( Subgrupos[Media] )
R Barra = AVERAGE ( Subgrupos[Amplitude] )
UCL X = [X Barra Barra] + 0.577 * [R Barra]
LCL X = [X Barra Barra] - 0.577 * [R Barra]
UCL R = 2.114 * [R Barra]
```

```py-r
--- python
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

dados = np.array([
    [3,4,3,5,4], [2,9,3,4,3], [4,5,4,3,5], [3,4,5,4,3], [5,4,3,4,5],
    [4,3,4,5,4], [3,5,4,3,4], [4,4,3,5,4], [5,3,4,4,3], [4,4,5,3,4],
], dtype=float)

medias = dados.mean(axis=1)
amplitudes = dados.max(axis=1) - dados.min(axis=1)
xbarbar = medias.mean()
rbar = amplitudes.mean()

A2, D3, D4 = 0.577, 0, 2.114  # constantes tabeladas para n=5
ucl_x, lcl_x = xbarbar + A2*rbar, xbarbar - A2*rbar
ucl_r, lcl_r = D4*rbar, D3*rbar

print(f"X̄̄ = {xbarbar:.3f}   R̄ = {rbar:.3f}")
print(f"Gráfico X-barra: UCL={ucl_x:.3f}  LCL={lcl_x:.3f}")
print(f"Gráfico R:       UCL={ucl_r:.3f}  LCL={lcl_r:.3f}")

fora_r = np.where(amplitudes > ucl_r)[0] + 1
fora_x = np.where((medias > ucl_x) | (medias < lcl_x))[0] + 1
print("Subgrupos fora de controle na Amplitude:", list(fora_r))
print("Subgrupos fora de controle na Média:", list(fora_x) or "nenhum")

# Paineis X-barra e R plotados, com os pontos fora de controle destacados em vermelho.
subgrupos = np.arange(1, len(medias) + 1)
fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(9, 7), sharex=True)

ax1.plot(subgrupos, medias, "o-", color="#00688f", linewidth=1.5, markersize=5)
for s in fora_x:
    ax1.plot(s, medias[s-1], "o", color="red", markersize=9, zorder=5)
ax1.axhline(xbarbar, color="#31803a", linestyle="-", linewidth=1.3, label=f"LC (X̄̄={xbarbar:.3f})")
ax1.axhline(ucl_x, color="#a5203a", linestyle="--", linewidth=1.2, label=f"LSC={ucl_x:.3f}")
ax1.axhline(lcl_x, color="#a5203a", linestyle="--", linewidth=1.2, label=f"LIC={lcl_x:.3f}")
ax1.set_title("Gráfico X-barra (médias dos subgrupos)")
ax1.set_ylabel("Média do subgrupo")
ax1.legend(loc="upper right", fontsize=8, framealpha=0.9)
ax1.grid(alpha=0.3)

ax2.plot(subgrupos, amplitudes, "o-", color="#d17a00", linewidth=1.5, markersize=5)
for s in fora_r:
    ax2.plot(s, amplitudes[s-1], "o", color="red", markersize=9, zorder=5)
ax2.axhline(rbar, color="#31803a", linestyle="-", linewidth=1.3, label=f"LC (R̄={rbar:.3f})")
ax2.axhline(ucl_r, color="#a5203a", linestyle="--", linewidth=1.2, label=f"LSC={ucl_r:.3f}")
ax2.axhline(lcl_r, color="#a5203a", linestyle="--", linewidth=1.2, label=f"LIC={lcl_r:.3f}")
ax2.set_title("Gráfico R (amplitude dos subgrupos)")
ax2.set_xlabel("Subgrupo")
ax2.set_ylabel("Amplitude")
ax2.legend(loc="upper right", fontsize=8, framealpha=0.9)
ax2.grid(alpha=0.3)
ax2.set_xticks(subgrupos)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

```py-r
--- python
%%R
dados <- matrix(c(
  3,4,3,5,4, 2,9,3,4,3, 4,5,4,3,5, 3,4,5,4,3, 5,4,3,4,5,
  4,3,4,5,4, 3,5,4,3,4, 4,4,3,5,4, 5,3,4,4,3, 4,4,5,3,4
), ncol = 5, byrow = TRUE)

medias <- rowMeans(dados)
amplitudes <- apply(dados, 1, function(r) max(r) - min(r))
xbarbar <- mean(medias)
rbar <- mean(amplitudes)

A2 <- 0.577; D3 <- 0; D4 <- 2.114
ucl_x <- xbarbar + A2*rbar; lcl_x <- xbarbar - A2*rbar
ucl_r <- D4*rbar; lcl_r <- D3*rbar

cat(sprintf("X-barra-barra = %.3f   R-barra = %.3f\n", xbarbar, rbar))
cat(sprintf("Grafico X-barra: UCL=%.3f  LCL=%.3f\n", ucl_x, lcl_x))
cat(sprintf("Grafico R:       UCL=%.3f  LCL=%.3f\n", ucl_r, lcl_r))
cat("Subgrupos fora de controle na Amplitude:", which(amplitudes > ucl_r), "\n")

# Conferencia com o pacote qcc, que ja embute as constantes A2/D3/D4.
# Revisao 2026: plot = FALSE foi trocado por plot = TRUE (e um segundo
# grafico "R" foi adicionado) para que os graficos X-barra e R sejam de
# fato desenhados aqui, e nao apenas os numeros dos limites.
library(qcc)
q  <- qcc(dados, type = "xbar", plot = TRUE)
qr <- qcc(dados, type = "R",    plot = TRUE)
cat("qcc - centro:", q$center, " limites X-barra:", q$limits, "\n")
```

**Minitab** (current version — check minitab.com): **Stat → Control Charts → Variables Charts for Subgroups → Xbar-R**, with the data in one column and subgroup size 5 (or the 5 values in separate columns). Under **Xbar-R Options → Tests**, select *Perform all tests for special causes* — the same steps cited in the text, which reproduced "Test Failed at points: 2" for the range chart.

*Verification note: all five methods converge — X̄̄≈3.98, R̄≈2.50, R chart's UCL≈5.29 — and all flag subgroup 2 (range 7) as out of control on the range, with the subgroup averages staying within limits — the same qualitative pattern described in the text ("Test Failed at points: 2"). R's `qcc` package independently confirms the same X-bar limits.*

### Practicing Control Chart Interpretation

With Minitab, building control charts simply requires following the steps described above and some practice to determine which control chart fits the situation and how to set up the data for the control chart. The hardest part is interpreting control charts to make valid business decisions or recommendations. In this section, you'll review control charts for a variety of real-world scenarios, and practice interpreting them.

**Help Desk Ticket Process**

An office's tech support tracks the number of tickets opened and closed each hour. This data is in the table below (19 hours of data, with tickets received and tickets completed per hour).

Management wants to know whether the help desk process is performing well, given only this information. A Six Sigma specialist can do a few things to provide management with a preliminary answer.

First, you can build an I-MR chart for the Tickets Completed data. Why use an I-MR chart? We don't have enough data to build an X-bar chart, because we'd only have a few subgroups.

The I-MR chart is shown below, and you can see there are no control failures, either for the moving range or for the number of tickets closed per hour.

<img alt="I-MR chart of Completed Tickets, with no points flagged (no test failures)" src="data:image/png;base64," style="max-width:700px;width:100%;height:auto;display:block;margin:0.6rem auto;"  />


Someone might point out, though, that a control chart of the number of tickets completed only tells us there isn't much deviation in the amount of work completed each hour, and that's true. This control chart doesn't factor in how much work came in each hour, and whether the help desk was keeping up with it.

So, a Six Sigma specialist can add another column to the data. This column keeps a running total of how many tickets, at that point in the day, remain open.

Building an I-MR chart from this new figure produces very different results.

```
Test Results for I Chart of Tickets Left Unresolved

<img alt="I-MR chart of Unresolved Tickets, with several points flagged for failing different control tests" src="data:image/png;base64," style="max-width:700px;width:100%;height:auto;display:block;margin:0.6rem auto;"  />


TEST 1. One point more than 3.00 standard deviations from center line.
Test Failed at points:  17

TEST 2. 9 points in a row on same side of center line.
Test Failed at points:  13

TEST 5. 2 out of 3 points more than 2 standard deviations from center line (on one side of CL).
Test Failed at points:  18

TEST 6. 4 out of 5 points more than 1 standard deviation from center line (on one side of CL).
Test Failed at points:  8, 9, 10, 12

```

Numerous tests fail at numerous points on the chart. Is that bad? Not necessarily, given an understanding of the process. The first five failing points do so because they're below the center line. That means the process was leaving fewer tickets open per hour than might be expected. Several reasons could explain such results:

- The team was being especially efficient at closing tickets during those hours.
- The team got unusually easy tickets to handle and close during those hours.
- The team closed tickets without actually resolving them.
- The team simply received fewer tickets to work.

The first two reasons are positive, and the third could point to a problem with the team. The last reason could be positive or negative: were there fewer tickets because everything was running better than normal, or was there a problem with the ticketing software?

All of these questions are worth investigating — they not only tell the team whether the process might be out of control, but also provide valuable business information.

The next two out-of-control points on this chart are due to an upward trend — something a help desk manager wouldn't want to see. They'd want to keep monitoring this chart, to see whether the process corrects itself or keeps trending upward.

**Running a Hypothesis Test**

Given all this information, a Six Sigma specialist might even run a hypothesis test, to accompany any control charts. They could run a 2-Sample T-Test, to determine whether the team is closing, on average, the same number of tickets that are being opened. If the answer is yes, then the help desk is likely performing well. If the answer is no, then the team can ask "how many tickets, on average, is the help desk not closing?"

The results of running the 2-Sample T-Test in Minitab are seen below.

```
Two-Sample T-Test and CI: Incoming Tickets, Complete Tickets

Two-sample T for Incoming Tickets vs Complete Tickets

                   N  Mean  StDev  SE Mean
Incoming Tickets  19  9.42   4.89      1.1
Complete Tickets  19  9.11   3.62     0.83

Difference = μ (Incoming Tickets) - μ (Complete Tickets)
Estimate for difference:  0.32
95% CI for difference:  (-2.52, 3.16)
T-Test of difference = 0 (vs ≠): T-Value = 0.23  P-Value = 0.822  DF = 33

```

It's true that, with a sample size of 19, the chance of a Type II Error is relatively high, and the p-value (0.822) is nowhere near enough to justify rejecting the null hypothesis that the mean is statistically the same between the incoming-tickets and completed-tickets data — but that doesn't prove the means are equal, only that the sample didn't provide enough evidence of a difference. Given this information, the Six Sigma team can accumulate more data, before running another test, to verify these results.

**Yarn Skeins**

At a company that produces yarn skeins for retail sale, each 244-yard skein features a particular color or color pattern. The company allows small dyeing defects, at a rate of 10 per 244-yard length of yarn, before the skein is considered overall defective.

A team was tasked with controlling this process's quality. This team reviews 10 sampled lengths of yarn each day, before they're wound into a skein, to determine the number of defects. Over several days, the team collects data and builds a control chart, to indicate whether its process is under control. The team generates the following data table (21 samples of 10 units each, with defect counts ranging from 2 to 27).

Since all the sample sizes are the same, and the team is concerned with the number of defects, it chooses to build a C chart in Minitab.

```
Test Results for C Chart of Defects Found

<img alt="C chart of Defects Found in yarn skeins, with points 2, 12, and 21 flagged in red for failing the test" src="data:image/png;base64," style="max-width:700px;width:100%;height:auto;display:block;margin:0.6rem auto;"  />


TEST 1. One point more than 3.00 standard deviations from center line.
Test Failed at points:  2, 12, 21

```

Based on three points failing the control tests, this process isn't fully under control and should be reviewed.

**Call Center Compliance**

A bank's call center monitors its employees for compliance with numerous federal regulations, as well as internal policies and procedures. The monitoring comes from a quality assurance team that randomly listens to phone calls and logs information about errors team members might make on the phone. Team members can make more than one error on each call; for example, a team member might forget to inform the caller that the call is being recorded, and fail to give the caller the correct information.

Over a 10-hour shift, the quality assurance team monitored calls every hour, and built the following data table (Hour, Calls Monitored, and Errors columns).

The sample size, indicated by the number of calls monitored each hour, isn't consistent in this example. Reasons for inconsistent subgroups, in this case, could be that the number of incoming calls varies each hour, and the quality assurance team only reviews a certain portion of the calls. It could also be that some calls take longer — and therefore take longer to review. Whatever the reason for the inconsistent subgroup sizes, it leads us to choose the U chart, which is concerned with the number of errors per unit. In this case, that would be calculated by dividing errors by calls monitored, creating rate or proportion data, so the actual sample size doesn't matter as much.

When entering the data into Minitab to build this control chart, Errors are the Variables, and Calls Monitored is the Subgroup size.

Minitab generates the following control chart.

<img alt="U chart of call-center Errors, with no points flagged (no test failures), with a stepped upper control limit due to unequal sample sizes" src="data:image/png;base64," style="max-width:700px;width:100%;height:auto;display:block;margin:0.6rem auto;"  />


You can see no test fails, which indicates the process is under control. You'll also notice the upper control limit appears to step up and down throughout the chart. That happens because each sample had a different size, so each upper control limit is calculated with a different value.

**What if call center management were especially concerned about a specific error?**

If call center management were concerned about PCI compliance (compliance with payment card industry regulations), they might want to dig deeper into the data, to see information about the number of errors related to PCI compliance. They could ask the quality assurance team to check a box while reviewing a call, indicating whether the call was PCI-compliant or not.

The new data table is seen below (Hour, Calls Monitored, Errors, and PCI Non-compliance columns).

Instead of being concerned with the number of errors per call, we want to understand the rate at which PCI errors occur. We can use a P chart for that purpose.

```
Test Results for P Chart of PCI Non-compliance

<img alt="P chart of PCI Nonconformity, with no points flagged for test failure, but with four of the last five points above the 0,10 proportion mark" src="data:image/png;base64," style="max-width:700px;width:100%;height:auto;display:block;margin:0.6rem auto;"  />


(no tests failed)

```

This chart is a great illustration of how a process under control can still be a problematic process. This process is under control, but four of the last five points are above the 0.10 proportion mark. That means, out of 10 samples, four had a failure rate of 10% or more with respect to PCI compliance.

In the banking world, PCI compliance problems can cost a lot of money, which means banking call centers will want to see PCI compliance error rates as close to zero as possible. This call center's process owner will likely take steps to reduce this process's average proportion, even though it's under control.

### Common Cause Versus Special Cause Variation

When selecting the control tests in Minitab, you'll notice we chose to run every test for special causes. This instructs Minitab to run every special-cause variation test — special-cause variation is that caused by something outside the normal expectations within a process.

Any process will have some amount of variation. The normal variation within a process — the variation caused by the process itself — is called common-cause variation. For example, a phone operator working at a call center will occasionally make a speaking or typing error while carrying out their job duties. That variation is accounted for on a control chart. However, an operator working too many hours, with a bad headset, or new to the job might make more than the normal amount of errors. That abnormality is likely to show up on a control chart, and is explained by special causes, like a defective headset.

### Additional Minitab Control Charts

Minitab offers a variety of other control charts. We've covered the most commonly used control charts in this chapter, but we briefly highlight a few others below.

**The I & MR (Within/Between) Chart**

Not to be confused with the I-MR (Individual Moving Range) chart mentioned earlier; the I & MR (Within/Between) chart provides a three-way chart, indicating variation within a group and between groups. You can use this chart when the variation between batches is high compared to the variation within batches, or when the variation isn't randomly distributed. For example, when working with a process spanning shifts, you might have subgroups within the shift groups, and differences might show up between shifts.

You can find this chart under Stat > Control Charts > Variables for Subgroups.

**Exponentially Weighted Moving Average**

The EWMA chart delivers an individuals and moving-range chart. This chart is rarely used in common statistical analysis, since it's hard to work with. Most often, the EWMA chart is used when dealing with automated data systems.

**Cumulative Sum**

The CUSUM chart handles the cumulative sums of each sample's deviations, relative to a target value. CUSUM is very effective at detecting a small deviation from a target, particularly in a process that's under control. Like EWMA, CUSUM isn't a commonly used control chart in most business settings.
